canonical_topic: Option writing as the market's limiting factor
definition: The scarce side of the options market is sellers (writers), not buyers, because buying an option has no downside beyond its cost while writing an option means accepting open-ended risk.
core_idea: Because option buyers face no risk beyond the premium paid, there is always ample demand to buy options; the real constraint on market activity is finding someone willing to write (sell) options and bear the associated risk. A fair option price is defined as one that fully compensates the writer for the risk taken on.
key_points: Option buyer demand is essentially unlimited since the only downside to owning an option is its cost.
The scarce resource in the options market is willing option writers/sellers, who take on open-ended risk.
The goal of option pricing, and the definition of a 'fair' option price, is a price that fully compensates the writer for the risk assumed.
relationships: Ties back to the asymmetric payoff concept: buyer's limited risk vs. writer's unlimited risk.
trading_implications: Fair-value option pricing should be evaluated from the writer's risk-compensation perspective, not merely from buyer demand.
